nu: Vitamin C, potassium, pectin fibre, quercetin, catechins
b: Soluble fibre feeds gut bacteria and slows sugar absorption; regular intake is linked to lower LDL cholesterol and lower type 2 diabetes risk.
m: Traditionally used for constipation and diarrhoea (pectin); peel polyphenols have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity.
r: Seeds contain amygdalin (release cyanide if crushed and eaten in large amounts). Raw apple can trigger oral allergy syndrome in birch-pollen allergy. Juice lacks fibre and acid erodes enamel.
s: Most pesticide residue sits on the skin, so wash well. Eat with the skin for most polyphenols and fibre.

nu: Potassium, vitamin B6, vitamin C, manganese, resistant starch (green)
b: Supports blood pressure, muscle and nerve function through potassium; quick, easily digested energy for exercise.
m: Green banana resistant starch used for diarrhoea and gut health; traditional remedy for stomach ulcers (plantain).
r: Latex-fruit syndrome: people allergic to natural rubber latex may react. High potassium matters for advanced kidney disease and some blood-pressure drugs (ACE inhibitors).
s: Ripeness changes the sugar profile: green is starchy and low-GI, spotted is sweeter and higher-GI.

nu: Vitamin C, folate, thiamine, hesperidin, potassium
b: One orange gives about the full daily vitamin C; improves iron absorption from plant foods and supports collagen and immunity.
m: Prevents scurvy. Hesperidin and naringenin are studied for blood-vessel function. Peel oil is used in aromatherapy.
r: Acidic: can worsen reflux and erode enamel. Citrus allergy exists. Grapefruit (not orange) interacts with many drugs.
s: Whole fruit beats juice: juice loses fibre and makes it easy to take in a lot of sugar fast.

nu: Vitamin C, vitamin A (beta-carotene), folate, copper, mangiferin
b: Rich in antioxidants and carotenoids for eye and skin health; fibre and enzymes aid digestion.
m: Ayurveda uses unripe mango for heat stroke and diarrhoea; mangiferin studied for anti-inflammatory and blood-sugar effects.
r: Skin and sap contain urushiol (same family as poison ivy), causing contact dermatitis in sensitive people. Can cross-react with cashew and pistachio allergy.
s: Called the king of fruits; over 1,000 varieties. Eat ripe and sweet or green and sour.

nu: Anthocyanins, vitamin K, vitamin C, manganese
b: Among the highest antioxidant fruits; studies link regular intake to better memory, blood pressure and insulin sensitivity.
m: Traditionally used for urinary health (similar to cranberry) and eyesight; evidence for night vision is weak.
r: Generally very safe. High vitamin K is only a concern for people on warfarin if intake changes suddenly.
t: North American Indigenous peoples ate them dried and fresh and used the plant medicinally.
u: Natural purple dye; jams and baking.
v: Trials show improved blood vessel function and modest memory gains in older adults. Cohorts link regular intake to lower type 2 diabetes risk.
s: Frozen berries are picked ripe and retain nutrients, often cheaper than fresh.

nu: Vitamin C, manganese, folate, ellagic acid, anthocyanins
b: Low calorie and low sugar; vitamin C and polyphenols support heart health and reduce inflammation.
m: Ellagitannins studied for anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory activity in lab work; human proof is limited.
r: One of the more common fruit allergens (Fra a 1, birch-related). Often top of lists for pesticide residue.
s: Not a true berry botanically; the seeds on the outside are the actual fruits.

nu: Vitamin K, vitamin C, resveratrol (skin), flavonoids
b: Red and purple grapes carry resveratrol and anthocyanins linked to heart and blood-vessel health.
m: Grape seed extract used for circulation and vein health; resveratrol studied for ageing and heart disease.
r: Toxic to dogs. Sugar is concentrated in raisins. Rare grape allergy (lipid transfer protein).
s: Wine benefits are mostly from the grape compounds, but alcohol harms outweigh them.

nu: Vitamin C, manganese, bromelain enzyme, vitamin B6
b: Bromelain helps protein digestion and may reduce swelling after surgery or injury.
m: Bromelain is used for inflammation, sinus swelling and wound healing; evidence is moderate.
r: Bromelain can irritate mouth and cause tingling; allergy possible. Interacts with blood thinners and some antibiotics. Unripe fruit can cause cramps.
s: Contains enzymes that break down proteins, which is why it stops gelatin from setting.

nu: Vitamin C, vitamin A, folate, papain enzyme, lycopene
b: Papain aids protein digestion; high vitamin C and carotenoids support skin, immunity and eyes.
m: Traditional digestive aid and wound dressing (green papaya); leaf extract used in dengue fever studies for platelet counts.
r: Unripe papaya latex may stimulate uterine contractions and should be avoided in pregnancy. Latex allergy cross-reactivity.
s: Ripe orange papaya is safe in pregnancy in normal amounts; the unripe green fruit is the concern.

nu: Monounsaturated fat, potassium, vitamin K, folate, vitamin E, fibre
b: Heart-healthy oleic acid; fat helps absorb fat-soluble vitamins from other foods; very high in fibre.
m: Seed and leaf used traditionally for diarrhoea and blood pressure; evidence is preliminary.
r: High calorie. Latex-fruit allergy cross-reactivity. Persin in leaves and skin is toxic to birds and some animals.
s: Technically a large berry. Ripens only after harvest.

nu: Punicalagins, vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, potassium
b: One of the richest polyphenol fruits; studies show improved blood pressure and artery function.
m: Juice studied for prostate and cardiovascular health; peel used traditionally for diarrhoea and worms.
r: Can interact with statins and blood-pressure medicines. Allergy is uncommon but real.
s: Ancient fruit mentioned in many cultures; the seeds (arils) are the edible part.

nu: Water (91%), lycopene, vitamin C, citrulline
b: Very hydrating; citrulline converts to arginine and may improve blood flow and reduce muscle soreness.
m: Citrulline studied for mild high blood pressure and erectile function.
r: Large amounts can cause bloating (FODMAP). Pollen-food allergy cross-reactivity with ragweed.
s: Red flesh has more lycopene than tomato by weight in some varieties; rind is edible and pickled in many cuisines.

nu: Vitamin C (higher than orange), vitamin K, vitamin E, actinidin enzyme
b: Three kiwis daily improved constipation in trials; high vitamin C supports immunity.
m: Studied for sleep quality, constipation and cold duration.
r: Common allergen with real risk of oral swelling or anaphylaxis; cross-reacts with latex and birch. Actinidin tingles the mouth.
s: Skin is edible and holds extra fibre; gold varieties are sweeter.

nu: Potassium, magnesium, copper, fibre, polyphenols
b: Concentrated natural energy and fibre; traditionally broken fast food; studies show late-pregnancy intake may ease labour.
m: Used in Middle Eastern medicine for constipation and as a tonic; polyphenols have antioxidant action.
r: Very high sugar and calorie density; portion size matters for diabetes. Sulfite preservatives may trigger asthma in some.
s: Medjool dates are larger and softer; dried-fruit calories add up fast.

nu: Vitamin C, citric acid, flavonoids, limonene (peel)
b: Citrate in lemon juice may help prevent kidney stones; vitamin C aids iron absorption.
m: Peel oil and juice used in folk remedies for colds and sore throats; evidence is limited.
r: Acid erodes enamel and aggravates reflux; peel oils can cause sun-sensitive skin reactions.
s: Squeeze on iron-rich plant foods like lentils to raise absorption.

nu: Medium-chain triglycerides, manganese, copper, selenium, fibre
b: Source of MCT fat and fibre; coconut water is a natural electrolyte drink.
m: Traditional uses include hydration for diarrhoea; lauric acid has antimicrobial activity in the lab.
r: Mostly saturated fat; raises LDL in many studies. Tree-nut allergy label in some countries although cross-reactivity is uncommon.
s: Mature flesh is fat-rich; young coconut water is low calorie.

nu: Vitamin C (about 4x orange), lycopene, potassium, fibre
b: Exceptional vitamin C and fibre; low glycemic impact for a sweet fruit.
m: Leaf tea used in many countries for diarrhoea and blood sugar; clinical evidence is early.
r: Seeds are hard and can lodge in diverticula (rare). Unripe fruit is astringent.
s: Pink-fleshed types contain lycopene.

nu: Vitamin C, potassium, vitamin B6, magnesium
b: Largest tree fruit in the world; young green jackfruit is a meat substitute high in fibre.
m: Leaves and seeds used in folk medicine for digestion and skin; research is limited.
r: Cross-reacts with birch pollen and latex allergy. Ripe fruit sugar is high.
s: One fruit can weigh over 30 kg and feed a family.

nu: Vitamin K, vitamin A, folate, iron, lutein, magnesium, nitrate
b: Rich in lutein for eye health and nitrate for blood pressure; very nutrient dense for its calories.
m: Studied for eye disease (AMD, cataract) and blood pressure.
r: High in oxalates: may contribute to kidney stones in prone people. Vitamin K interacts with warfarin. Iron is non-heme (absorb better with vitamin C).
s: Cooking reduces oxalate and increases mineral availability; raw has more vitamin C.

nu: Vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, sulforaphane, fibre
b: Sulforaphane activates detox enzymes; regular cruciferous intake is linked to lower cancer risk.
m: Sulforaphane studied for cancer prevention, H. pylori, and autism symptoms (early research).
r: Glucosinolates can suppress thyroid iodine uptake in large raw amounts if iodine intake is low. Gas and bloating for many.
s: Light steaming preserves myrosinase enzyme and sulforaphane; boiling destroys it. Sprouts have the highest levels.

nu: Beta-carotene (vitamin A), vitamin K, biotin, potassium
b: Eye and skin health via vitamin A; cooked carrots release more carotene.
m: Seed oil and juice used traditionally; beta-carotene prevents night blindness from vitamin A deficiency.
r: Very large intake turns skin orange (carotenemia), harmless. Birch pollen cross-reactive allergy.
s: Purple and red carrots have anthocyanins and lycopene.

nu: Lycopene, vitamin C, potassium, vitamin K, folate
b: Cooked tomato makes lycopene far more absorbable; linked to lower prostate cancer and heart disease risk.
m: Lycopene studied for prostate health and UV skin protection.
r: Acidic; can trigger reflux. Nightshade sensitivity claims lack strong evidence. Tomato allergy (profilin) occurs.
s: Heat and a little oil increase lycopene absorption.

nu: Potassium, vitamin C, vitamin B6, resistant starch (cooled)
b: Very filling and high in potassium; cooled potatoes form resistant starch that feeds gut bacteria.
m: Raw potato juice used folk-wise for stomach ulcers; limited evidence.
r: Green or sprouted potatoes contain solanine and chaconine, toxic and bitter. Frying produces acrylamide. High glycemic index when hot.
s: Eat the skin for fibre and minerals; store in a cool dark place.

nu: Beta-carotene, vitamin C, manganese, potassium, fibre
b: Orange types are among the richest vitamin A sources; lower glycemic index when boiled.
m: Leaves and tubers used for anaemia and diabetes control traditionally; purple types high in anthocyanins.
r: High in oxalate for stone-prone people. Large vitamin A from supplements is a different matter from food.
s: Boiling gives a lower GI than baking.

nu: Quercetin, vitamin C, B6, chromium, prebiotic fructans
b: Prebiotic fibre feeds gut bacteria; quercetin has anti-inflammatory action; linked to bone health.
m: Traditional cough syrups; studied for blood sugar and blood pressure support.
r: High FODMAP: causes bloating and IBS symptoms for many. Can worsen reflux. Toxic to dogs and cats.
s: Red onion carries more quercetin and anthocyanins.

nu: Allicin (when crushed), manganese, vitamin B6, vitamin C, selenium
b: Studied for modest blood-pressure and cholesterol lowering; antimicrobial.
m: Used for 5,000 years for infection; supplements reduce blood pressure by a few points in trials.
r: Can increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and before surgery. Heartburn and body odour. High FODMAP.
t: Used in ancient Egypt, Greece, China and India for infections, heart health and digestion.
u: Soldiers' and labourers' ration in antiquity; insect repellent; core flavouring worldwide.
v: Meta-analyses show garlic preparations lower blood pressure a few mmHg in people with hypertension and cut total cholesterol slightly. Links to lower stomach and bowel cancer in population studies are not confirmed by trials. Can add to bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
s: Crush and rest for 10 minutes before heating to form more allicin.

nu: Vitamin K, vitamin C, vitamin A, lutein, calcium
b: Extremely nutrient dense; calcium absorption is better than from spinach because it has low oxalate.
m: Glucosinolates studied for cancer prevention; lutein for eyes.
r: Vitamin K interaction with warfarin. Goitrogens in raw large amounts. May be high in pesticide residue.
s: Massage raw kale with oil to soften it.

nu: Vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, glucosinolates
b: Cheap, filling and rich in vitamin C; fermented as sauerkraut or kimchi adds probiotics.
m: Cabbage leaves are used topically for breast engorgement; juice studied for stomach ulcers.
r: Gas and bloating (raffinose). Goitrogenic if eaten in very large raw amounts.
s: Red cabbage has anthocyanins; fermenting boosts vitamin K2 in some forms.

nu: Vitamin C, vitamin K, choline, folate, sulforaphane
b: Low carb alternative to rice or potato; provides choline for brain and liver.
m: Cruciferous compounds studied for cancer prevention.
r: Gas, bloating; thyroid caution as for broccoli in iodine deficiency; purine content is moderate for gout.
s: Roasting makes it sweet and nutty.

nu: Nitrate, folate, manganese, betalains, potassium
b: Dietary nitrate converts to nitric oxide, lowering blood pressure and improving exercise stamina.
m: Juice studied for blood pressure; betalains have anti-inflammatory effects.
r: Beeturia (pink urine and stool) is harmless. High oxalate and may affect kidney stones. Can lower blood pressure too much with medication.
s: Leaves are edible like chard.

nu: Water (95%), vitamin K, potassium, cucurbitacins
b: Extremely hydrating and low calorie; peel has silica and vitamin K.
m: Used topically for skin soothing; cooling in traditional medicine.
r: Cucurbitacins can make some cucumbers bitter and cause digestive upset. Cross-reactive pollen allergy.
s: Eat with the peel; wash or peel if waxed.

nu: Vitamin C (about 3x orange), vitamin A, vitamin B6, capsanthin
b: Highest vitamin C among common vegetables; carotenoids support eyes.
m: Antioxidant compounds studied for eye and heart health.
r: Nightshade sensitivities are rare; pepper allergy cross-reacts with birch and latex.
s: Red peppers are ripe green peppers and are sweeter and richer in nutrients.

nu: Beta-carotene, vitamin C, potassium, vitamin E
b: Low calorie but full of carotenoids; seeds are a separate rich food (zinc, magnesium).
m: Seeds studied for prostate and bladder health; flesh for eyes and skin.
r: Generally safe. Pumpkin allergy is rare.
s: Pumpkin seeds are covered under nuts and seeds.

nu: Fibre, manganese, nasunin (skin), potassium
b: Skin anthocyanin nasunin has antioxidant action; low calorie and filling.
m: Traditionally used for blood sugar and cholesterol; evidence is limited.
r: Nightshade family; contains solanine in small amounts and nicotine traces. Allergy and oral reactions occur. Absorbs lots of oil when fried.
s: Salting is no longer needed with modern varieties.

nu: Vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, magnesium, mucilage fibre
b: Soluble mucilage helps blood sugar and cholesterol; gentle on the gut.
m: Okra water is used in folk medicine for blood sugar; early research only.
r: High oxalate and fructans. May reduce absorption of metformin.
s: Cook fast or dry-roast to reduce sliminess.

nu: Vitamin C, folate, charantin, polypeptide-p
b: One of the most studied foods for blood sugar; very low calorie.
m: Used in Ayurveda and Chinese medicine for diabetes; compounds act like insulin in lab studies.
r: Can cause hypoglycaemia with diabetes drugs. Unsafe in pregnancy (miscarriage risk). Seeds can cause favism-type reaction in G6PD deficiency.
s: The bitterness is part of its action; salt and soak to reduce it.

nu: Folate, vitamin K, vitamin C, inulin, asparagine
b: Excellent folate source; prebiotic fibre; gentle diuretic effect.
m: Root used traditionally for urinary health.
r: Makes urine smell (harmless, genetic). Purine content for gout. Allergy to the Liliaceae family is rare.
s: White asparagus is grown without light and is milder.

nu: Vitamin K, vitamin C, folate, manganese, plant protein, fibre
b: High protein for a vegetable; high fibre keeps blood sugar stable.
m: Pea protein studied for blood pressure and fullness.
r: Legume family allergy possible; FODMAPs cause gas; purines moderate.
s: Frozen peas are picked and frozen within hours and retain nutrients.

nu: Heme iron, zinc, vitamin B12, B6, niacin, selenium, creatine, complete protein
b: Best-absorbed iron and zinc source; B12 is essential for nerves and blood; high-quality protein for muscle.
m: Used for iron-deficiency anaemia and recovery. Collagen-rich cuts (bone broth) are traditional tonics.
r: Processed and large amounts of red meat are linked to colorectal cancer risk (WHO group 2A for red meat). Saturated fat in fatty cuts. Alpha-gal syndrome (tick-borne) causes delayed allergy to red meat. Iron overload in haemochromatosis.
s: Grass-fed beef has more omega-3 and CLA. Cook to a safe internal temperature (steaks 63 °C, mince 71 °C).

nu: Iron, zinc, vitamin B12, selenium, niacin, CLA
b: Rich complete protein and highly bioavailable iron and zinc.
m: Mutton soup is used in many traditions for weakness and postpartum recovery.
r: Saturated fat; red meat cancer link; alpha-gal allergy; uric acid for gout.
s: Fat carries much of the flavour. Rare cuts need food-safety care.

nu: Thiamine (B1, very high), selenium, B6, B12, zinc, phosphorus
b: One of the richest thiamine sources; lean cuts are good complete protein.
m: No major medicinal use; pork collagen and gelatin used in broths.
r: Must be fully cooked (63 °C) to avoid Trichinella and tapeworm (Taenia solium). Fatty cuts add saturated fat. Prohibited in Islam and Judaism. Alpha-gal cross-reaction.
s: Tenderloin and loin are the leanest cuts.

nu: Iron, potassium, B12, zinc, low saturated fat
b: Leaner than beef and lamb with less saturated fat; high in iron.
m: Used in tonic soups in South Asia and the Caribbean.
r: Red meat considerations apply; low fat dries quickly, so slow-cook.
s: Most commonly eaten red meat worldwide.

nu: Iron, zinc, B12, B6, niacin, low fat
b: Very lean, high protein, low fat game meat.
m: No special medicinal claims; used in traditional tonics.
r: Wild game may carry lead from bullets, parasites, and chronic wasting disease risk (do not eat sick animals). Cook well.
s: Cook gently to keep it from toughening.

nu: Vitamin A (retinol, huge), B12, folate, copper, iron, riboflavin
b: Among the most nutrient-dense foods: one serving exceeds daily B12, A, copper and riboflavin needs.
m: Historically used to treat anaemia and night blindness; vitamin A deficiency cure.
r: Excess retinol is harmful, especially in pregnancy (birth defects); eat in small, occasional portions. Copper excess in Wilson disease; purines for gout; cholesterol.
s: Limit to about one small portion a week; avoid during pregnancy.

nu: Protein, B vitamins, sodium, nitrites
b: Tasty protein, but the nutrition profile is dominated by salt and fat.
m: None.
r: WHO group 1 carcinogen (processed meat); high sodium; nitrosamines. Linked to bowel cancer, heart disease and high blood pressure.
t: None; not used medicinally.
u: Curing preserved meat for sea voyages and winter before refrigeration.
v: IARC (2015) classified processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1): about 50 g a day raises colorectal cancer risk roughly 18%. Also linked to higher heart disease and blood pressure through salt.
s: Treat as an occasional food; look for no-added-nitrite products.

nu: Lean protein, niacin, B6, selenium, phosphorus
b: Highest protein per calorie among common meats; good for weight management and muscle building.
m: Chicken soup shows mild anti-inflammatory activity in studies and eases cold symptoms.
r: Salmonella and Campylobacter risk: cook to 74 °C and avoid cross-contamination. Antibiotic resistance concerns in farming. Woody breast quality issues.
s: Never wash raw chicken (spreads bacteria).

nu: Iron, zinc, B vitamins, more fat than breast
b: Juicier, more iron and zinc than breast and forgiving to cook.
m: As above.
r: Same food-safety cautions; skin adds saturated fat.
s: Dark meat has more myoglobin.

nu: Protein, selenium, niacin, B6, tryptophan
b: Very lean protein; tryptophan is a serotonin and melatonin precursor.
m: Folk idea of turkey sleepiness is mostly overeating, not tryptophan.
r: Cook to 74 °C; deli turkey is high in sodium and a Listeria risk for pregnancy.
s: Dry if overcooked; brine or cook with moisture.

nu: Iron, selenium, B vitamins, monounsaturated fat
b: Rich flavour; fat is relatively high in unsaturated fats compared with other animal fats.
m: Used in Chinese medicine as a cooling food.
r: High in calories and fat with skin; cook to 74 °C.
s: Duck fat is prized for roasting potatoes.

nu: Iron, B vitamins, selenium, zinc
b: Small, tender, high-protein bird; quail eggs are eaten as well.
m: Quail eggs used in some Asian traditions for allergy relief (unproven).
r: Allergic reactions to quail eggs are possible; cook thoroughly.
s: Quail is usually eaten whole.

nu: Iron, selenium, B vitamins, monounsaturated fat
b: Rich dark meat; high protein.
m: Goose fat is a traditional chest rub folk remedy (unproven).
r: Fat-heavy with skin; cook through.
s: Seasonal festive meat in much of Europe.

nu: Omega-3 EPA and DHA, vitamin D, B12, selenium, astaxanthin
b: Two servings a week are linked to fewer heart attacks and better brain health; best food source of vitamin D after oily fish.
m: Omega-3 reduces triglycerides; studied for depression, inflammation and arthritis.
r: Fish allergy is one of the major allergens. Farmed fish may carry PCBs and contaminants; mercury low. Raw: parasites (Anisakis) unless frozen.
t: Indigenous Pacific Northwest and Nordic peoples valued it as a vital, strengthening food.
u: Central to Indigenous ceremony and trade; smoked and cured for preservation.
v: Omega-3 EPA and DHA lower triglycerides. Eating fish about twice a week is linked to fewer coronary deaths; supplement trials for prevention in healthy people are mixed.
s: Wild salmon is leaner; farmed has more omega-3 by weight but also more fat.

nu: Lean protein, selenium, niacin, B12, omega-3 (less than salmon)
b: Very high protein and low fat; selenium supports thyroid and antioxidant function.
m: Omega-3 effects as other fish (smaller amounts).
r: Mercury: limit large tuna (bluefin, bigeye) especially in pregnancy and children. Scombroid (histamine) poisoning if poorly stored.
s: Canned light (skipjack) tuna is lower in mercury than albacore.

nu: Omega-3, calcium (edible bones), vitamin D, B12, selenium, CoQ10
b: Small fish low on the food chain: high omega-3, very low mercury, edible bones give calcium.
m: Recommended for heart health and bone health.
r: High purines (gout); salt in canned; fish allergy.
s: One of the most sustainable seafood choices.

nu: Lean protein, iodine, B12, phosphorus, selenium
b: Very low fat, mild flavour; good for iodine; liver oil is a separate supplement.
m: Cod liver oil (vitamin A, D, omega-3) is a traditional tonic for bones and joints.
r: Fish allergy (parvalbumin). Cod liver oil can overdose vitamin A and D.
s: Overfished in some regions; look for certified stocks.

nu: Omega-3, vitamin D, B12, selenium, iodine
b: Rich oily fish with very high omega-3; cheap and widely available.
m: Omega-3 for heart and brain; studied for inflammation.
r: King mackerel is high in mercury (avoid in pregnancy); Atlantic and chub mackerel are low. Scombroid poisoning if not kept cold.
s: Eat fresh or smoked quickly after catch.

nu: Protein, iodine, selenium, B12, astaxanthin, choline
b: Very lean, high protein, rich in iodine and astaxanthin.
m: Chitosan from shells used in supplements (limited evidence).
r: Shellfish allergy (tropomyosin) is common and can cause anaphylaxis. Cholesterol is high but saturated fat is low. Farmed shrimp has environmental and labour concerns.
s: Cooks in minutes; overcooking makes it rubbery.

nu: Zinc (highest of any food), B12, copper, selenium, iron
b: Single oysters deliver many times the daily zinc; strong immunity and wound-healing support.
m: Traditional aphrodisiac; zinc supports testosterone and immune function.
r: Raw oysters can carry Vibrio and norovirus; avoid raw if pregnant, immunocompromised or with liver disease. Shellfish allergy.
s: R-month rule is outdated with modern refrigeration but warm waters raise risk.

nu: Protein, B12, zinc, copper, selenium, omega-3
b: Low fat, high protein with good trace minerals.
m: Chitin and glucosamine from shells used in joint supplements.
r: Shellfish allergy; shell fragments; sodium in processed crab; cadmium in brown meat.
s: Brown meat is richer but holds more contaminants.

nu: Lean protein, phosphorus, selenium, niacin
b: Affordable lean white fish.
m: None specific.
r: Low in omega-3 and higher in omega-6; farming quality varies; fish allergy.
s: Mild flavour makes it a good beginner fish.

nu: Copper, B12, riboflavin, selenium, taurine
b: Good protein with copper and B12; low fat when not fried.
m: Taurine content studied for heart health.
r: Shellfish and mollusc allergy; high cholesterol; fry adds fat; high purines.
s: Cook either very quickly or for a long time; in between is tough.

nu: Protein, selenium, zinc, copper, B12
b: Lean protein with rich minerals.
m: None specific.
r: Shellfish allergy; cholesterol; high sodium in boiled; tomalley can concentrate toxins.
s: Cook live or fresh only; spoils quickly after death.

nu: Iron, B12, manganese, selenium, omega-3
b: Rich in iron and B12; sustainable bivalve.
m: Green-lipped mussel extract is used for arthritis (some evidence).
r: Shellfish allergy; algal toxins (red tide) can cause paralytic or diarrhetic poisoning; discard unopened shells.
s: Filter feeders; buy from certified waters.

nu: Carbohydrate energy, manganese, folate (enriched), low fibre
b: Gentle on the stomach; staple energy for half the world; fortified rice supplies B vitamins.
m: Rice water and congee used for diarrhoea and recovery.
r: Higher glycemic index; polished rice lacks fibre; rice can carry inorganic arsenic (rinse, cook in extra water). Bacillus cereus from reheated rice left out.
s: Cool and reheat quickly to avoid food poisoning; cooling also creates resistant starch.

nu: Fibre, magnesium, manganese, selenium, B vitamins
b: Whole grain with bran: more fibre and minerals; linked to lower diabetes risk.
m: Studied for blood sugar and cholesterol.
r: Higher arsenic in bran; phytic acid reduces mineral absorption (soaking helps).
s: Takes longer to cook; fats in bran make it go off sooner.

nu: Fibre, B vitamins, iron, magnesium, selenium, lignans
b: Whole grain reduces risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
m: Wheat bran for constipation; wheatgrass is a folk tonic (limited evidence).
r: Contains gluten: unsafe in coeliac disease, wheat allergy and non-coeliac gluten sensitivity. FODMAP fructans cause IBS symptoms.
s: Whole grain labels should say 100% whole.

nu: Beta-glucan fibre, manganese, phosphorus, thiamine, avenanthramides
b: Beta-glucan lowers LDL cholesterol and blunts blood sugar; very filling.
m: Oat baths soothe eczema and itchy skin; oats studied for cholesterol (approved health claim).
r: Often cross-contaminated with gluten unless labelled gluten-free; rare avenin sensitivity in coeliacs.
t: Used in Europe as porridge for convalescents; colloidal oatmeal soothes itchy skin.
u: Livestock feed, skin-care products, bedding and baking.
v: Oat beta-glucan (about 3 g/day) lowers LDL cholesterol by roughly 5 to 7%, supported by an approved health claim in the EU and US.
s: Steel-cut and rolled oats have a lower GI than instant.

nu: Complete protein, magnesium, iron, folate, manganese, flavonoids
b: One of few plant foods with all essential amino acids; gluten-free.
m: Studied for blood sugar and cholesterol.
r: Saponins on seeds taste bitter (rinse well); oxalate; rare allergy.
s: A pseudocereal (seed), staple of the Andes for 5,000 years.

nu: Beta-glucan, selenium, manganese, magnesium, fibre
b: Among the highest fibre grains; lowers cholesterol and blood sugar.
m: Barley water is a traditional remedy for urinary and digestive issues; barley grass used as a supplement.
r: Contains gluten (hordein); FODMAP.
s: Hulled barley keeps more fibre than pearled.

nu: Lutein, zeaxanthin, folate, vitamin C, thiamine, resistant starch
b: Yellow corn carries eye-protective carotenoids; whole kernels give fibre.
m: Corn silk tea used for urinary issues.
r: Niacin is bound unless treated with alkali (nixtamalization), so maize-only diets cause pellagra. Mycotoxin (aflatoxin) contamination in stored corn.
s: Masa made with lime frees niacin and improves calcium.

nu: Magnesium, phosphorus, B vitamins, iron, polyphenols
b: Gluten-free, drought-resistant grain; steady blood sugar response.
m: Studied for diabetes management.
r: Goitrogens in large amounts with low iodine intake.
s: Ancient grain; includes pearl, foxtail, proso.

nu: Antioxidant tannins, iron, phosphorus, B vitamins
b: Gluten-free, high antioxidant and slow digesting.
m: Studied for cholesterol and glycaemic control.
r: Tannins reduce mineral absorption.
s: Pops like popcorn.

nu: Rutin, magnesium, manganese, copper, complete amino acids
b: Gluten-free seed with rutin for blood vessels.
m: Rutin is used for varicose veins and capillary fragility.
r: Buckwheat allergy can be severe and cross-reacts with latex; fagopyrism (photosensitivity) in animals.
s: Not related to wheat.

nu: Fibre (arabinoxylan), manganese, phosphorus, lignans
b: Very filling bread grain with low glycemic response and strong gut benefits.
m: Studied for satiety and blood sugar.
r: Gluten (secalin); ergot fungus poisoning historically.
s: Dark rye bread is dense and sour.

nu: Calcium, iron, resistant starch, manganese, protein
b: Gluten-free, high calcium and iron for a grain.
m: Traditional food in Ethiopia and Eritrea for stamina.
r: Phytates; generally safe.
s: Used for injera flatbread; the smallest grain in the world.

nu: Calcium (very high), iron, polyphenols, methionine
b: Richest grain source of calcium; slow digesting; good for bones and diabetes.
m: Traditional weaning food in India; studied for blood sugar.
r: Oxalate and phytate; goitrogens if iodine is low.
s: Sprouting improves mineral availability.

nu: Plant protein, folate, iron, potassium, fibre, polyphenols
b: High protein and fibre; supports heart health, blood sugar and weight; folate for pregnancy.
m: Lentil intake linked to lower heart disease and diabetes risk.
r: Lectins and phytates reduced by soaking and cooking; gas and bloating (oligosaccharides); purines for gout.
s: Cooks without soaking; red lentils cook in 10–15 minutes.

nu: Protein, folate, manganese, iron, resistant starch, fibre
b: Fills you up; shown to improve cholesterol and gut health.
m: Traditionally used for digestion; hummus is part of the Mediterranean diet.
r: Gas; legume allergy; raw chickpea is not safe (cook).
s: Aquafaba (cooking liquid) whips like egg white.

nu: Anthocyanins, folate, iron, magnesium, fibre, plant protein
b: Black seed coat anthocyanins; very high fibre; slow steady blood sugar response.
m: Studied for cholesterol and blood sugar.
r: Must be cooked: raw or undercooked beans contain phytohaemagglutinin. Gas.
s: Soak and boil vigorously for 10 minutes.

nu: Fibre, folate, iron, potassium, molybdenum, protein
b: High protein and fibre; resistant starch feeds gut bacteria.
m: Studied for weight control and blood sugar.
r: Raw or slow-cooker undercooked beans cause severe vomiting (lectin). Gas. Purines.
s: Never cook in a slow cooker from raw without boiling first.

nu: Complete plant protein, isoflavones, iron, folate, omega-3, vitamin K
b: Complete protein; isoflavones studied for menopausal symptoms, bone and heart health.
m: Soy foods may lower LDL modestly; fermented soy (natto) has vitamin K2.
r: One of the major allergens. Goitrogens in iodine deficiency. Phytoestrogens in large supplements; interacts with thyroid medicine absorption.
t: China counted it among the five sacred grains; TCM used it for digestion and as a tonic.
u: Soy sauce, oil, animal feed, soil nitrogen-fixing crop rotation, industrial uses.
v: Meta-analyses show soy protein lowers LDL by about 3 to 4% and isoflavones modestly ease hot flushes. Soy foods have not been shown to raise breast cancer risk.
s: Fermented forms (miso, tempeh, natto) are easiest to digest.

nu: Complete protein, calcium (if set with calcium sulfate), iron, isoflavones, manganese
b: Low-calorie, high-quality plant protein; calcium-set tofu supports bones.
m: Soy isoflavones studied for menopause and cardiovascular health.
r: Soy allergy; high in oxalate for stone formers; shop for non-GMO if preferred.
s: Pressing removes water so it crisps.

nu: Protein, probiotic bacteria (fermentation), B vitamins, iron, magnesium
b: Fermented soybean cake with better mineral absorption, prebiotics and gut benefits.
m: Fermentation makes isoflavones more bioavailable.
r: Soy allergy; histamine in fermented foods; cook to be safe.
s: Originated in Java, Indonesia.

nu: Protein, folate, manganese, magnesium, vitexin
b: Easy to digest legume; sprouts are used raw and cooked.
m: Cooling food in Ayurveda and Chinese medicine; studied for blood sugar.
r: Raw sprouts carry Salmonella/E. coli risk; cook for pregnancy and young children.
s: Used in dal, sprouts and desserts.

nu: Protein, niacin, vitamin E, magnesium, resveratrol, monounsaturated fat
b: Heart-healthy fats and protein; early peanut introduction reduces allergy in infants.
m: Studied for heart health.
r: One of the most dangerous allergens: severe and life-threatening reactions. Aflatoxin mould in poor storage.
s: Botanically a legume not a tree nut.

nu: Protein, folate, vitamin K, iron, isoflavones
b: Young soybeans: protein, fibre and folate in one snack.
m: Same soy isoflavone interest as soy.
r: Soy allergy; goitrogen caution in iodine deficiency.
s: Eat the beans not the pod.

nu: Protein, folate, potassium, iron, fibre
b: A staple lentil of India, high in protein and fibre.
m: Leaves used in Ayurveda for jaundice and wounds.
r: Legume allergy; G6PD caution; purines.
s: Used for sambar and dal.

nu: Vitamin E, magnesium, monounsaturated fat, calcium, riboflavin, fibre
b: Lower LDL cholesterol and help weight control; vitamin E protects cells.
m: Used traditionally for skin and brain; studied for cholesterol.
r: Tree nut allergy; bitter almonds contain cyanide-producing compounds (not sold raw); calorie dense.
s: Soak overnight for easier digestion.

nu: ALA omega-3, polyphenols, copper, manganese, vitamin B6
b: Best plant source of omega-3 (ALA); linked to better heart and brain health.
m: Studied for cognitive function and cholesterol.
r: Tree nut allergy is common and severe; very calorie dense; rancid if stored warm.
t: Persian and Chinese traditions used them as a brain, kidney and longevity tonic.
u: Husk dye, ink, hard wood for furniture and gunstocks, oil for painting.
v: Trials show walnuts reduce LDL cholesterol modestly and improve blood vessel function; large cohorts link nut eating to lower heart disease. Cognition trials are inconclusive.
s: Store in the fridge.

nu: Copper, magnesium, zinc, manganese, iron
b: Mineral rich and creamy; lower in fat than most nuts.
m: Cashew apple and shell oil used in folk medicine.
r: Tree nut allergy (high risk); raw cashews have urushiol in shell (sold roasted); oxalate.
s: Never sold truly raw: steam heating removes the toxic shell oil.

nu: Vitamin B6, thiamine, potassium, lutein, fibre, protein
b: Highest protein of the tree nuts and rich in lutein; linked to good gut bacteria.
m: Studied for blood pressure and eye health.
r: Tree nut allergy; cross-reactive with cashew and mango; salted versions add sodium.
s: Shelling slows eating and reduces intake.

nu: Selenium (very high), magnesium, copper, vitamin E
b: One or two nuts reach the selenium daily need; supports thyroid and immunity.
m: Selenium for thyroid function.
r: Too much selenium is toxic (selenosis: hair loss, nerve damage); limit to 1–3 nuts a day; naturally radioactive trace radium.
s: Eating more than about 4 a day on a regular basis is not advised.

nu: Vitamin E, manganese, copper, folate, monounsaturated fat
b: Heart-healthy fat; vitamin E and folate.
m: Studied for cholesterol.
r: Tree nut allergy; birch pollen cross-reactivity.
s: Basis of Nutella and praline.

nu: Monounsaturated fat (palmitoleic acid), thiamine, manganese
b: Highest in monounsaturated fat; cholesterol-friendly.
m: Studied for cholesterol.
r: Tree nut allergy; very calorie dense; toxic to dogs.
s: Native to Australia (Queensland/NSW).

nu: Manganese, thiamine, zinc, polyphenols, monounsaturated fat
b: High antioxidant nut; supports heart health.
m: Studied for LDL cholesterol.
r: Tree nut allergy; calorie dense.
s: Native to North America.

nu: Fibre, ALA omega-3, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus
b: Extreme fibre (about 34 g per 100 g) and plant omega-3.
m: Traditional Aztec energy food; studied for blood sugar and regularity.
r: Dry seeds can swell and cause throat blockage: soak first. Allergy possible; large fibre doses cause bloating.
s: Soaking makes a gel (chia pudding).

nu: ALA omega-3, lignans, fibre, thiamine, magnesium
b: Best food source of lignans; supports cholesterol and bowel regularity.
m: Ground flax studied for hot flashes, blood pressure and breast health.
r: Must be ground to absorb; raw seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides (small); phytoestrogen caution; can lower absorption of medicines taken at the same time.
s: Store ground flax in the fridge; it goes rancid.

nu: Zinc, magnesium, iron, protein, phosphorus, vitamin E
b: Excellent magnesium and zinc source; studied for prostate, bladder and sleep.
m: Traditional remedy for intestinal worms; used for prostate (BPH).
r: Calorie dense; fibre bloating; allergy uncommon.
s: Shelled are called pepitas.

nu: Vitamin E (very high), selenium, magnesium, B vitamins
b: One of the best vitamin E sources; good for skin and cells.
m: Studied for cholesterol and inflammation.
r: Seed allergy; calorie dense; salted types are high in sodium; cadmium accumulation.
s: Sunflower butter is a nut-free spread.

nu: Calcium, copper, iron, lignans (sesamin), magnesium
b: Very high calcium and copper; sesamin supports cholesterol.
m: Black sesame used in Chinese medicine for hair and kidney; sesame oil used in Ayurveda massage.
r: A major allergen in many countries (labelled); calorie dense.
s: Tahini is ground sesame paste.

nu: Complete protein, omega-3 and omega-6 in balance, magnesium, iron, zinc
b: Complete plant protein with a good omega ratio.
m: Studied for skin and heart health.
r: Trace THC (very low) may affect drug tests with heavy intake; allergy rare.
s: Hemp hearts are the shelled seeds.

nu: Vitamin C, manganese, copper, fibre, low fat
b: Unusual low-fat, starchy nut; good for fibre and vitamin C.
m: Traditional use for digestive health.
r: Latex-fruit cross-reactivity; tannins; needs cooking.
s: Pierce skin before roasting to avoid bursting.

nu: Complete protein, choline, B12, selenium, vitamin D, lutein, riboflavin
b: Nutrient dense; choline supports brain and liver; lutein protects eyes. One egg is about 6 g protein.
m: Used in many traditions as a restorative food.
r: Egg allergy is common in children (most outgrow it). Salmonella if raw or runny in vulnerable groups. Dietary cholesterol matters less than once thought, but caution with diabetes and familial hypercholesterolaemia.
s: Yolk holds most nutrients; cook until firm for pregnancy and frail people.

nu: Calcium, protein, vitamin B12, riboflavin, iodine, phosphorus
b: Best-absorbed calcium source; supports bones and growth.
m: None specific.
r: Cow milk allergy (children); lactose intolerance (most adults worldwide); saturated fat; acne link in some studies.
s: Fortified milk adds vitamin D.

nu: Probiotics, calcium, protein, B12, iodine
b: Live cultures support gut balance; easier for many lactose intolerant people.
m: Probiotics studied for antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and IBS.
r: Dairy allergy; added sugar in flavoured versions; histamine.
s: Look for “live and active cultures”.

nu: Calcium, protein, vitamin K2, B12, zinc
b: Concentrated calcium and protein; aged cheese has very little lactose.
m: Vitamin K2 supports bones and arteries (studied).
r: High saturated fat and sodium; Listeria risk in unpasteurised soft cheese for pregnancy; tyramine triggers migraines.
s: Small portions are nutritious.

nu: Protein, calcium, phosphorus, casein
b: Staple vegetarian protein in South Asia; slow-digesting casein.
m: Used in Ayurveda as a cooling food.
r: Dairy allergy; high saturated fat; sodium in commercial kinds.
s: Made by curdling milk with acid.

nu: Vitamin A, vitamin E, butyrate, vitamin K2 (grass-fed)
b: Fat-soluble vitamins; flavour carrier.
m: Butyrate helps the gut lining.
r: Saturated fat raises LDL; calorie dense; dairy allergy (low protein so lactose tolerant).
s: Cultured butter has more flavour.

nu: Butyric acid, vitamins A, E, K, stable at high heat
b: Lactose and casein free; high smoke point; core food of Ayurveda.
m: Ayurveda uses it for digestion, skin and as a carrier of herbs; evidence is limited.
r: Pure saturated fat; calorie dense.
s: Clarified butter with milk solids removed.

nu: Dozens of probiotic strains and yeasts, calcium, B12, protein
b: More diverse than yogurt; studied for lactose digestion and gut health.
m: Traditional Caucasian health drink.
r: Dairy allergy; contains trace alcohol; immune-suppressed people should check with a doctor.
s: Water kefir is dairy free.

nu: Calcium, protein, B12, phosphorus
b: Lower sodium and fat than many cheeses; good protein.
m: None.
r: Dairy allergy; fresh unpasteurised carries Listeria risk.
s: Buffalo mozzarella is richer.

nu: Curcumin, manganese, iron, vitamin B6 (powder)
b: Curcumin is anti-inflammatory; black pepper (piperine) increases absorption by up to 2000%.
m: Standard in Ayurveda; studied for arthritis, inflammation and digestion. Curcumin supplements show modest pain relief.
r: High supplement doses can cause liver injury (rare), interact with blood thinners and diabetes drugs, and worsen gallstones. Oxalate.
t: Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine used it for wounds, jaundice, joint inflammation and digestion.
u: Yellow dye and food colouring; used in Hindu wedding and religious ritual; natural preservative in curries.
v: Meta-analyses of randomised trials show curcumin modestly reduces knee osteoarthritis pain and some inflammation markers. Absorption is poor unless taken with piperine or fat. No proven anti-cancer effect in people; rare liver injury reported with high-dose supplements.
s: Culinary doses are tiny so benefits come from supplements; use with fat and pepper.

nu: Gingerols, shogaols, manganese, magnesium
b: Proven for nausea (pregnancy, chemotherapy, motion); reduces muscle soreness.
m: Standard remedy for nausea and colds; studied for menstrual pain and osteoarthritis.
r: High doses may cause heartburn and thin the blood; caution with warfarin and before surgery; gallstones.
t: TCM and Ayurveda use it for nausea, colds, joint pain and poor digestion.
u: Spice, tea, ginger beer, candied sweets, preserved gari in Japan.
v: Randomised trials support a modest benefit for pregnancy nausea and chemotherapy nausea, and some benefit for osteoarthritis pain. Evidence for blood sugar and weight is weaker and inconsistent.
s: Fresh or dried both work; dried is stronger by weight.

nu: Cinnamaldehyde, manganese, calcium, polyphenols
b: May lower fasting blood glucose slightly; antimicrobial and antioxidant.
m: Used in TCM and Ayurveda for digestion and colds; studied for type 2 diabetes.
r: Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin (liver toxic at high intake): prefer Ceylon cinnamon for daily use. Mouth irritation.
t: Ayurveda, TCM and ancient Egypt used it for digestion, colds and blood sugar; used in embalming.
u: Perfume, incense, embalming and flavouring.
v: Meta-analyses show small, inconsistent drops in fasting glucose. Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which can harm the liver at high intakes; Ceylon has far less.
s: Ceylon (true cinnamon) is low in coumarin.

nu: Piperine, manganese, vitamin K, iron
b: Piperine boosts absorption of nutrients and drugs (turmeric, selenium, B vitamins).
m: Used for digestion and cough in Ayurveda.
r: Can interact with medicines by changing absorption (e.g. phenytoin, propranolol); irritates reflux.
s: Known as the king of spices.

nu: Iron, manganese, cuminaldehyde, thymol
b: Supports digestion; among richest herb sources of iron.
m: Studied for IBS and blood sugar; used for indigestion.
r: May lower blood sugar; heartburn; allergy possible.
s: Toast the seeds before grinding.

nu: Eugenol, manganese, vitamin K, fibre
b: Highest antioxidant spice by weight; eugenol is a natural anaesthetic.
m: Clove oil used for toothache in dentistry and folk practice.
r: Large amounts of clove oil are toxic to the liver (especially in children); blood-thinning effect.
s: Use whole cloves sparingly.

nu: Manganese, cineole, iron, magnesium
b: Aids digestion and breath; small studies for blood pressure.
m: Used in Ayurveda for digestion, nausea and as a breath freshener.
r: Large doses may worsen gallstone pain.
s: Third most expensive spice by weight after saffron and vanilla.

nu: Soluble fibre (galactomannan), iron, saponins, 4-hydroxyisoleucine
b: May lower blood sugar and boost milk supply in breastfeeding.
m: Used for diabetes and lactation; studied for blood sugar and testosterone.
r: Can lower blood sugar too much with medication; may cause uterine contractions in pregnancy; maple-syrup body odour; legume allergy.
t: Ayurveda, Egyptian and Chinese medicine used it to raise milk supply, aid digestion and manage diabetes.
u: Maple-like flavouring, curry spice blends, animal fodder.
v: Small trials suggest lower blood glucose and HbA1c. Evidence for increased breast milk is weak and mixed. Cross-reacts with legume allergy.
s: Soak seeds to reduce bitterness.

nu: Vitamin K, eugenol, manganese, vitamin A, flavonoids
b: Anti-inflammatory essential oils; holy basil (tulsi) is a stress adaptogen.
m: Tulsi studied for stress, blood sugar and immunity.
r: Estragole in large amounts is a concern for pregnancy; vitamin K interaction with warfarin.
s: Add at the end of cooking.

nu: Menthol, vitamin A, vitamin C, rosmarinic acid
b: Peppermint oil capsules relieve IBS symptoms and bloating.
m: Peppermint is the best-studied herb for IBS and tension headache.
r: Menthol can worsen GERD (relaxes sphincter); allergy; toxic to infants near the face (peppermint oil).
s: Spearmint is milder.

nu: Vitamin K, vitamin C, vitamin A, antioxidants
b: Fresh leaves are rich in vitamin K; seeds aid digestion.
m: Used for digestion; studied for blood sugar and heavy metal binding (limited).
r: Soapy taste to people with an OR6A2 gene variant; allergy in celery-mugwort family.
s: The seeds are coriander; the leaves are cilantro in the US.

nu: Vitamin K (very high), vitamin C, vitamin A, apigenin, folate
b: Very rich in vitamin K and vitamin C; breath freshening.
m: Folk diuretic and for kidney health; apigenin is studied.
r: Large medicinal doses may stimulate the uterus; vitamin K and warfarin interaction; oxalate.
s: Flat-leaf has more flavour than curly.

nu: Carnosic acid, rosmarinic acid, iron, calcium
b: Antioxidants reduce harmful compounds when grilling meat.
m: Aroma studied for memory and mood; used for hair growth in folk practice.
r: High doses may trigger seizures in epilepsy; avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy.
s: Marinate meat with rosemary to reduce carcinogens from charring.

nu: Crocin, safranal, manganese, vitamin C
b: Trials show mild-to-moderate benefit for depression and PMS.
m: Used for mood, eye health and aphrodisia; studied for depression.
r: Very high doses are toxic and can cause miscarriage; allergic reactions.
s: Costs more than gold by weight: 150,000 flowers per kg.

nu: Capsaicin, vitamin C, vitamin A, B6
b: Capsaicin speeds metabolism slightly and is analgesic; linked to lower mortality in observational studies.
m: Capsaicin cream treats neuropathic pain, arthritis and shingles pain.
r: Burning pain, reflux and IBS flares; can irritate skin and eyes; rare allergic reactions; extreme intake can damage the gut.
s: Heat is measured in Scoville units: bell pepper 0, jalapeño up to 8,000, Carolina Reaper over 1.5 million.

nu: Selenium, magnesium, omega-3, glucosinolates, calcium
b: Selenium and magnesium; glucosinolates produce the heat when crushed.
m: Mustard plasters were a classic chest remedy; studied for cancer prevention.
r: Mustard is a major allergen (labelled in the EU and Canada); skin burns from poultices.
s: Sinigrin gives the pungency.

nu: Vitamin A, vitamin C, calcium, iron, protein, quercetin
b: Dense in vitamins and protein; used to fight malnutrition in tropical regions.
m: Used for diabetes, anaemia, and breast-milk supply; evidence modest.
r: Root and bark can be toxic (spirochin); avoid in pregnancy; may lower blood sugar and pressure.
s: Called the drumstick or miracle tree.

nu: Selenium, riboflavin, niacin, potassium, ergothioneine, B5
b: Low calorie; a unique antioxidant (ergothioneine); a vitamin D source if exposed to UV light.
m: Polysaccharides studied for immunity.
r: Raw mushrooms contain agaritine (small amount; cook them); mushroom allergy; FODMAP mannitol.
s: The most widely grown mushroom in the world.

nu: Lentinan (beta-glucan), copper, selenium, B vitamins, vitamin D (UV)
b: Lentinan is used as an immune adjuvant in cancer care in Japan; supports cholesterol.
m: Long used in Chinese medicine for immunity and longevity.
r: Shiitake dermatitis (flagellate rash) if eaten raw or undercooked; allergy; always cook.
s: Dried shiitake have much more umami.

nu: Niacin, riboflavin, ergothioneine, potassium, lovastatin (natural statin)
b: Contains natural lovastatin which may lower cholesterol; rich in B vitamins.
m: Studied for cholesterol and immunity.
r: Rare allergy to spores; cook thoroughly.
s: Easy to grow at home on coffee grounds.

nu: Niacin, thiamine, copper, potassium, fibre
b: Low calorie noodle-like mushroom.
m: Used in Asian cuisine for health.
r: Listeria outbreaks have been linked to raw enoki; always cook.
s: Cook before eating.

nu: Hericenones, erinacines (stimulate nerve growth factor), beta-glucans
b: Small trials suggest benefits for mild cognitive impairment and mood.
m: Used in Chinese medicine for digestion and brain; research is early.
r: Allergy possible; limited long-term safety data.
t: Chinese and Japanese traditions used it for digestion and mental focus; Buddhist monks drank it before meditation.
u: Prized as a meaty 'vegetarian seafood' texture in cooking.
v: Only small human trials exist, such as a 16-week Japanese trial in mild cognitive impairment, with promising but unreplicated results. No large randomised trials yet.
s: Tastes like crab or lobster when cooked.

nu: Fructose, glucose, trace enzymes, antioxidants, methylglyoxal (Manuka)
b: Soothes cough better than some cough medicines in children over 1; antibacterial wound dressing (medical-grade).
m: Medical-grade honey is used for wounds and burns; folk antimicrobial.
r: Never give to infants under 12 months (botulism). Still sugar: raises blood glucose. Pollen allergy cross-reactivity.
t: Ancient Egypt, Greece and Ayurveda used it on wounds and for coughs and sore throats.
u: Sweetener, preservative, mead, and beeswax for candles and cosmetics.
v: Systematic reviews find honey modestly better than usual care for children's cough (over 1 year); medical-grade honey helps some burns and wounds. Never give to infants under 12 months (botulism risk).
s: Raw honey may crystallise naturally; Manuka is graded by MGO or UMF.

nu: Oleic acid, polyphenols (oleocanthal), vitamin E, vitamin K
b: Core of the Mediterranean diet; polyphenols are anti-inflammatory; linked to lower heart disease.
m: Oleocanthal has ibuprofen-like anti-inflammatory activity.
r: Calorie dense; rancid oil loses benefits; olive allergy is rare.
t: Mediterranean cultures used it as a skin salve, wound dressing and mild laxative.
u: Lamp fuel, soap, anointing in religious ritual, cosmetics.
v: The PREDIMED trial found a Mediterranean diet rich in extra virgin olive oil cut major cardiovascular events by about 30%. Large cohorts link higher intake to lower heart disease and all-cause death.
s: Store in the dark; fresher is better.

nu: Lauric acid, medium-chain triglycerides, saturated fat
b: Heat stable for cooking; MCTs are quickly used for energy.
m: Used topically for skin and hair.
r: About 82% saturated fat: raises LDL cholesterol. Health claims are overstated.
s: Use sparingly, not as a health food.

nu: Flavanols, magnesium, iron, copper, theobromine
b: Flavanols improve blood flow and blood pressure; mood lift; high in magnesium and iron.
m: Studied for blood pressure and cognition.
r: Caffeine and theobromine; contains lead and cadmium traces in some products; sugar and calorie dense; toxic to dogs; migraines in some.
s: Choose higher cocoa and an ounce a day at most.

nu: Catechins (EGCG), L-theanine, caffeine (about 25–45 mg per cup), manganese
b: Calm alertness from caffeine with L-theanine; EGCG antioxidant; linked to lower heart disease.
m: Studied for weight, heart and brain health; traditional in China and Japan.
r: Caffeine; reduces iron absorption if drunk with meals; rare liver injury from concentrated extract supplements.
t: China used it for alertness, digestion and as a general tonic for thousands of years.
u: Japanese tea ceremony; Buddhist meditation aid; tea is a daily social drink.
v: Large Japanese cohorts link regular green tea to lower cardiovascular death. Trials show small drops in LDL cholesterol and blood pressure; weight loss effect is small. High-dose extract supplements are linked to liver injury.
s: Per cup brewed (about 100 g of tea liquid).

nu: Caffeine, chlorogenic acids, magnesium, riboflavin
b: Three to four cups a day are linked to lower risk of type 2 diabetes, liver disease and Parkinson's.
m: Studied for liver protection and alertness.
r: Anxiety, insomnia, reflux, raised blood pressure briefly; limit 400 mg caffeine; avoid heavy use in pregnancy; boiled unfiltered coffee raises LDL.
t: Sufi circles in Ethiopia and Yemen used it for wakefulness during prayer.
u: Coffee ceremonies (Ethiopia), social ritual, fuel for the Arab and Ottoman coffeehouses.
v: Reviews of cohort studies link 3 to 4 cups a day to lower risk of type 2 diabetes, Parkinson's disease, liver disease and all-cause death, though mostly observational. Caffeine disturbs sleep and anxiety; limit to about 200 mg a day in pregnancy.
s: Per brewed cup, black.

nu: Iodine, vitamin B12 (small), vitamin A, folate, protein, fucoxanthin
b: Iodine for thyroid; protein-rich for a plant; omega-3 in small amounts.
m: Seaweed polysaccharides studied for gut health.
r: Excess iodine (especially kelp) can cause thyroid problems; heavy metals (arsenic in hijiki); sodium.
s: Kelp is far higher in iodine than nori.

nu: Protein, iron, phycocyanin, B vitamins, gamma-linolenic acid
b: Dense in protein and iron; phycocyanin is an antioxidant; NASA considered it for space.
m: Studied for cholesterol, allergic rhinitis and blood pressure.
r: Contamination with microcystins; can worsen autoimmune disease; phenylketonuria caution; B12 in spirulina is inactive analogue.
s: Eaten in small daily amounts of 1 to 5 g.

nu: Probiotics (unpasteurised), isoflavones, manganese, vitamin K, copper
b: Fermented soy paste that supports gut health and umami.
m: Traditional breakfast soup in Japan for digestion.
r: Very high sodium; soy allergy; thyroid caution.
s: Add at the end of cooking to preserve probiotics.

nu: Probiotics (Lactobacillus), vitamin C, vitamin K, fibre, capsaicin
b: Fermented cabbage with live cultures; supports gut microbiome diversity.
m: Studied for cholesterol and weight.
r: High sodium; histamine; may include fish sauce (not vegan); gas.
s: Korea has over 200 varieties.

nu: Probiotics, vitamin C, vitamin K, fibre
b: Fermented cabbage rich in lactic acid bacteria; historically prevented scurvy on ships.
m: Studied for digestion.
r: High sodium; histamine and tyramine (MAOI interaction); raw only is probiotic.
s: Buy refrigerated unpasteurised for live cultures.

nu: Acetic acid, trace potassium
b: Small studies show it can reduce post-meal blood sugar.
m: Folk use for blood sugar and weight; claims are overstated.
r: Always dilute: can damage tooth enamel and the throat; may worsen gastroparesis; interacts with diabetes and diuretic drugs.
s: A tablespoon in water is the maximum typically studied.

nu: Manganese, riboflavin, zinc, polyphenols
b: Slightly more minerals than white sugar; still sugar.
m: None.
r: High in sugar; dental decay; spikes blood glucose.
s: Grade by colour: darker is stronger tasting.

nu: Iron, magnesium, potassium, molasses trace minerals
b: Unrefined cane sugar with trace minerals; traditional sweetener in South Asia.
m: Used in Ayurveda for digestion and as an iron source (small).
r: Still sugar; high blood glucose effect; not a health food.
s: Often used with ginger for winter drinks.

nu: Protein, B12, iron, zinc, chitin fibre, omega-3
b: Very high protein and B12 with a much smaller environmental footprint than livestock.
m: No special medicinal uses.
r: Shellfish and dust mite allergy cross-reactivity; chitin may bother some; contamination if wild-collected.
s: Eaten by over 2 billion people worldwide.

nu: Vitamin A (beta-carotene), vitamin C, potassium, fibre
b: Rich in carotenoids for eye and skin health.
m: Kernel (xingren) used in TCM for cough and asthma.
r: Raw kernels release cyanide: people have been poisoned. Dried apricots often contain sulphites.
t: TCM uses the processed kernel to ease cough; seeds pressed for oil.
u: Kernel oil in cosmetics; amaretti flavour.
v: Cochrane found no proof that laetrile (amygdalin) treats cancer, and it can cause cyanide toxicity.
s: Dried apricots are concentrated in sugar and potassium.

nu: Vitamin C, vitamin A (carotenoids), potassium, polyphenols
b: Low calorie, hydrating, provides carotenoids.
m: Kernel (taoren) used in TCM for blood stasis and constipation.
r: Peach allergy often involves lipid transfer proteins and can be severe; kernels contain amygdalin.
t: TCM uses the seed to move blood and ease constipation; peach blossom for skin.
